newsitem.title: GERMANY: BHF sees commodity prices settling at high levels.
newsitem.headline: BHF sees commodity prices settling at high levels.

text.p: Commodities prices should undergo consolidation at high levels in 1997 on the basis of global economic growth of around four percent, a report from BHF-Bank said on Friday.
But price rises would be limited because the supply of industrial raw materials was likely to expand in a "textbook" response to the high prices already achieved.
Crude oil prices may average slightly below $20 per barrel after $20.5 in 1996 because of an easing of the recent tightness, the bank said.
The prospect of continued Iraqi oil exports and some OPEC quota excesses should be outweighed by a fall in seasonal consumption in the northern hemisphere.
In food commodities, the bank predicted 1997 price rises in tight coffee markets and in grains, where stocks were still low.
Grain prices last year rose by 21 percent, oilseeds and oils by 13 percent while combined cocoa, coffee and sugar prices were off 19 percent, the bank said.
It based the figures on a 28-product commodities index developed by the HWWA Institute for Economic Research, Hamburg, which measures dollar prices against 1975.
Non-ferrous metals prices lost 16 percent following exaggerated price increases in 1994 and 1995, especially in aluminium and nickel, BHF said.
Copper prices also plummeted in a crisis sparked by unauthorised dealings by a Sumitomo trader, although lead prices rose due to especially strong seasonal battery demand.
BHF said gold bullion had no prospects of returning to 1996 levels in the short term because further central bank sales could not be ruled out.
Gold, which ranged between $367 and $416 per ounce in 1996, recently hit a four-year low of $337.

BHF noted the European statistics body Eurostat had accepted central bank sales as legitimate means to cut state debt under the Maastricht criteria, but had also stressed that they could not count towards reducing deficits.
